title: Measuring transferable wind-power dynamics with explicit event protocols

abstract: Wind-power event catalogues connect production dynamics to forecasting and flexibility decisions. Their usefulness depends on how detection rules define intervals and how representations preserve the trajectories within them. We evaluate this measurement process across seven wind-farm archives containing 333 turbines. A primary benchmark of five farms and 17 detector configurations provides 1.54 million complete event shapes and 1.47 million matched test comparisons. Ordered 25-point trajectories achieve cross-detector normalized mutual information of 0.590–0.698, compared with 0.024–0.067 after event-row permutation, demonstrating shared grouping information across detector-defined intervals. In the 100-epoch learned comparison, adding a signed channel gives mean NMI/ARI of 0.709/0.815, while TCN gives 0.734/0.823 across the five primary farms. External Greek and SDWPF archives extend the tests to 144 additional turbines; the transferred TCN achieves mean agreement of 0.626 in SDWPF. Human review illustrates how V-shaped and inverted-V trajectories combine large internal excursions with small endpoint changes. Controlled experiments improve TimesNet and KAN-AD event F1 by 0.162 and 0.182 through interval grouping beyond threshold calibration. Real forecasting experiments show how event weighting reallocates accuracy toward large ramps and changes scenario cost. Together, these results establish an explicit route from event definition and temporal correspondence to representation selection and task-specific evaluation.
highlights: Seven wind-farm archives connect event measurement with external evaluation.
Temporal correspondence exposes shared structure across event protocols.
Signed and sequence-aware encoders preserve orientation-dependent structure.
Interval calibration improves localization with fixed detector scores.
Event-weighted forecasting reveals a trade-off between ramp error and cost.
